short: The sum of all values divided by how many there are.
long: It is very sensitive to extreme values: a few very high wages pull it up. If the mean is far above the median, there is inequality at the top.
example: If four people earn €1,000 and one earns €11,000, the mean is €3,000 but almost nobody earns that.

short: The “middle” value: half fall below it and half above.
long: It represents the typical worker better than the mean, because it is not dragged around by the extremes.
example: In the example above the median is €1,000.

short: Percentile N is the value that leaves N% of the population below it.
long: P10 describes the low end of the scale and P90 the high end. The distance between them measures wage inequality.
example: With a P90 of €52,000, only one in ten employees earns more.

short: Divides the population into four equal parts: the lower one leaves 25% below it and the upper one 75%.
long: Between the lower and the upper quartile lies the central half of employees.

short: What the worker earns before IRPF (income tax) and Social Security contributions are deducted.
long: The net amount that reaches the bank account is considerably lower. Here every wage is gross annual.

short: The wage measured in each year’s euros, without correcting for inflation.
long: It can rise every year and still buy less if prices rise faster.

short: The nominal wage corrected for price rises: it measures how much you can buy with it.
long: If it rises, you gain purchasing power; if it falls, you lose it even if your payslip is bigger. We calculate it ourselves: nominal wage ÷ price index.
example: If you earn 3% more and prices rise 5%, your real wage falls by 1.9%.

short: The quantity of goods and services you can buy with a given amount of money.
long: When there is inflation, the same money buys less and less.

short: The lowest monthly wage that can legally be paid for a full-time job.
long: It is set every year by royal decree. Here it is shown in euros per year (14 payments).

short: Consumer Price Index: how much the price of a representative basket of what households consume changes.
long: Positive = inflation (prices rise, money buys less). Around 2% is considered stable; above 5% it already hurts; below 0 is deflation. This version compares December with the previous December.
example: With a CPI of +3%, a basket that cost €100 last year costs €103.

short: A version of the CPI calculated with common EU rules, so that countries can be compared.
long: It is published by groups (food, housing, transport...) and here the annual average rate is used. It does not exactly match INE’s CPI.

short: A general and sustained rise in prices.
long: The European Central Bank considers inflation close to 2% to be stable.

short: The value, at each year’s prices, of all final goods and services a country produces in a year.
long: It grows both when more is produced and when what is produced becomes more expensive. To compare different years prices have to be corrected: that is real GDP.

short: What is produced, measured at constant prices, that is, without the effect of inflation.
long: Its annual change is “economic growth”. Positive = the economy produces more; negative = it produces less. Two negative quarters in a row are usually called a recession.

short: Turns each series into a common scale: the base-year value becomes 100 and the rest is expressed relative to it.
long: A 120 means 20% more than in the base year. It lets you compare in one chart things measured in different units. It is our own calculation.

short: How much a value changes compared with the previous year, in %.
long: This is what is called the “year-on-year rate”. Our own calculation when we start from a series in levels.

short: How much a value has changed from the base year to each year, in %.
long: A cumulative +25% in 2024 means the value is 25% higher than in the base year. It is our own calculation.

short: The average pace of growth per year between two dates (compound rate).
long: It is the constant growth that would give the same final result. Our own calculation.

short: An INE index that tracks the purchase price of homes, new and second-hand.
long: It does not give euros per square metre: it gives the trend. A 120 against another year means 20% more expensive. Here we use the annual average.
example: If the IPV rises 12% and wages 3%, buying a home becomes harder and harder on the same wage.

term: Years of wages to buy a home*
short: How many years of gross wages a typical 80 m² home would cost, with no mortgage.
long: We calculate it ourselves: 80 m² × appraised value per m² ÷ gross annual wage. It is a low estimate: it uses the appraisal (below the sale price), the wage of one person, and assumes saving all of it. No buyer saves 100% of their wage, so the real time is considerably longer. For market prices and household income, the official measure is the Bank of Spain’s (7.1 years in 2024).
example: With an appraised value of €1,900/m² and a wage of €29,500, an 80 m² home costs 5.2 years of wages. If you save 15% of that wage each year, you would need more than 35 years.

short: The value an appraisal company assigns to a home so that it can be granted a mortgage.
long: The Ministry of Housing publishes its average per m². It is not the price at which homes sell or the advertised price: it is usually lower.
example: A flat appraised at €150,000 may be advertised at €175,000.

short: Average rent of flats with a contract declared to the tax authorities, in euros per month or per square metre.
long: We calculate it ourselves: the 2022 level from the Ministry of Housing (SERPAVI) carried to other years with INE’s IPVA index. It includes all contracts in force, including old ones, which is why it rises less than today’s adverts (on Idealista, rent per m² in Spain is around €15 in 2026 versus the €7.8 of 2022 in this series).
example: If the average rent of a flat in Madrid was €738 in 2022 and the index rises 6% to 2024, the series shows about €782.

short: An INE index that tracks how much rents change, using tax data on all contracts.
long: It includes old contracts, which are rarely updated: that is why it rises less than the rents signed today.

short: Labour Force Survey: INE’s quarterly survey of around 65,000 families that measures how many people work, look for work or are inactive.
long: It is the official source of the unemployment rate. It is not the same as registered unemployment, which counts those who sign up with the SEPE (public employment service).

short: Percentage of the labour force (those who work or look for work) that has no job.
long: A rate of 10% means one in ten active people is looking for a job without having one. It does not count those who have stopped looking.
example: With 25 million active people and 10% unemployment there are 2.5 million unemployed.

short: Percentage of the population aged 16 and over that has a job.
long: It complements unemployment: unemployment can fall because there are more jobs or because people stop looking. The employment rate tells the two cases apart.

short: Percentage of the population aged 16 and over that works or is looking for work.
long: If it rises, more people are joining the labour market (for example women or immigrants).

short: People who usually live in a territory, on 1 January of each year.
long: When the population grows, GDP or total spending can rise without each person being better off. That is why we look “per capita”.

short: GDP divided by the number of residents.
long: Useful for comparing the size of the economy while removing the effect of there being more people. Our own calculation: GDP ÷ population on 1 January.

short: Measures inequality with a number between 0 (everyone earns the same) and 100 (one person takes it all).
long: For wages, values around 30 are usual in Europe. If it rises, the distribution becomes more unequal.

short: Compares the highest earners with the lowest: D9 leaves 90% below it and D1 leaves 10%.
long: A D9/D1 of 3.8 means that someone at the limit of the best-paid 10% earns 3.8 times what someone at the limit of the worst-paid 10% earns.

short: Percentage of employees whose hourly earnings are below two thirds of the median.
long: It is a measure of low-paid work relative to the rest: if it rises, the share of workers on low wages compared with the typical one grows.

short: Household Budget Survey: INE asks thousands of households what they spend their money on.
long: It shows how much housing, food or transport weigh in the spending of an average family.

short: Living Conditions Survey: INE measures households’ income, poverty and deprivation.
long: The survey year is not the income year: the income is from the previous year.

short: European indicator of risk of poverty or social exclusion: it adds income poverty, severe material deprivation and low work intensity.
long: It is a relative measure: if everyone earns more, the poverty threshold rises too.

short: GDP is shared among labour (compensation of employees), capital and the self-employed (surplus) and the State (net taxes).
long: If labour’s share falls while GDP rises, growth reaches wages less.

short: What public administrations spend on education.
long: It is usually expressed in euros and as a percentage of GDP so it can be compared across years and countries.

short: A period in which the economy contracts.
long: It is usually identified when real GDP falls in two consecutive periods.

short: What each sector adds to production: what it sells minus what it buys from others to produce.
long: GDP is the sum of the value added of all branches plus net taxes on products (such as VAT). That is why a sector weighs more on value added than on GDP.
